summary:
Ruth opens "In the days when the judges ruled" (1:1), when famine drives Elimelech of Bethlehem, his wife Naomi, and their two sons to the neighboring country of Moab. Within about ten years all three men are dead. Naomi starts home and urges her Moabite daughters-in-law to stay behind; Orpah does, but Ruth answers with a pledge: "wherever you go, I will go, and wherever you live, I will live; your people will be my people, and your God will be my God" (1:16). Back in Bethlehem, Naomi — whose name means "pleasant" — asks to be called Mara, "bitter" (1:20). A word that recurs is the Hebrew hesed, loyalty beyond obligation, rendered "loving devotion" in Naomi's blessing (1:8) and "kindness" later (2:20; 3:10).

Ruth goes out to glean — gathering grain the harvesters leave behind, a provision Israel's law commands for the poor and the foreign resident (Leviticus 19:9–10; Deuteronomy 24:19) — and "she happened to come" to a field belonging to Boaz, a relative of Elimelech (2:3). God works no miracles and speaks no lines in this book; the narrator credits Him directly only with ending the famine (1:6) and granting Ruth conception (4:13), and readers have long taken its "chance" meetings as providence. At Naomi's direction Ruth goes to the threshing floor by night and asks Boaz to act as her kinsman-redeemer — Hebrew goel, the nearest relative responsible to buy back family land and continue a dead man's line (Leviticus 25:25; Deuteronomy 25:5–6). A nearer relative holds first claim, but at the town gate he declines, sealing it by handing over his sandal, a custom the narrator himself explains (4:7).

Boaz marries Ruth, and the women of Bethlehem bless the LORD for Naomi's grandson, born of a daughter-in-law "better to you than seven sons" (4:15). The book closes with a genealogy: the child, Obed, "became the father of Jesse, the father of David" (4:17). The law had barred Moabites from the assembly of the LORD (Deuteronomy 23:3); this Moabite widow becomes King David's great-grandmother, and Ruth stands among the women Matthew names in his genealogy of Jesus (Matthew 1:5).
